opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's interesting, because at the time it didn't feel like a huge bet, at least not in the way people might think about it now. Spark came out of the AMPLab at Berkeley, and by the time we started Databricks in 2013 it already had real traction. People were using it, there was a community forming around it, and we could see that it solved a real pain point. Hadoop MapReduce was the dominant paradigm, but it was slow and awkward, especially for iterative workloads like machine learning and for interactive queries. Spark was often an order of magnitude faster and much easier to program. So we had strong signals that the technology was better.

The harder question was really about the business. Can you build a company around an open source project? Back then, the dominant model was the Red Hat model: support, services, maybe some proprietary add-ons. And frankly, we didn't think that was a great business. Early on we made what I think was one of the most important decisions, which was to bet on the cloud. We said, we're going to offer Spark as a hosted service in the cloud. That was not obvious in 2013. Most enterprises weren't ready to put their data in the cloud, and a lot of people told us we were too early. Many of our customers initially wanted on-prem deployments, and we said no, which was painful because we were turning away revenue.

But we believed that the cloud was where things were going, and that delivering software as a service was a fundamentally better way to capture value from open source. You're not just selling the code, which anyone can download, you're selling the operational expertise, reliability, security, and integration. That's much harder to replicate.

The other piece is that we never thought of it as just betting on Spark the project. We thought of it as betting on a broader trend: that data was going to keep growing, that more and more value would come from processing it, and especially from machine learning and AI on top of it. Spark was the best vehicle for that at the time. And over time the company expanded well beyond Spark, with Delta Lake, MLflow, the lakehouse architecture, and so on. So Spark was the wedge, but the real bet was on data and AI in the cloud.

And honestly, there's also a bit of luck and timing. When you start a company, you have conviction, but you don't really know. You make the best decision you can with the information you have, and then you have to execute very hard to make it right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Spark already had traction, was better for key workloads, and was the best vehicle for Databricks’ broader data and AI opportunity.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes choosing a cloud strategy despite customer resistance and turning away on-prem revenue, based on the belief that SaaS was the stronger business strategy.

r003.rationale: The candidate says Databricks never viewed the bet as limited to Spark, describes Spark as the wedge, and notes the company’s expansion into Delta Lake, MLflow, and lakehouse architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, honestly, at the time it didn't feel like a bet in the way people describe it now. When we started Databricks in 2013, Spark was already an open source project that had been around for a few years at the AMPLab at Berkeley, and it was gaining traction. People were downloading it, using it in production, showing up to meetups. So we weren't betting on an idea, we were betting on something that was already working, and the question was more about how to build a company around it.

But there were a couple of things we did think hard about. One was whether to keep Spark fully open. We decided very early that the project had to stay with the Apache Software Foundation, that we wouldn't fork it or hold back features. That was risky from a business point of view, because anyone could take the code, and in fact the big cloud providers eventually did. But we believed that the value of Spark came from the community, and if we tried to control it, we would have killed the thing that made it valuable.

The second thing was that we didn't want to be a Spark company, strictly speaking. We wanted to be the company that made data and AI simple for organizations, and Spark was the engine that got us started. So the bet was really on the thesis that unified data processing, where you could do SQL, streaming, machine learning in one system, would matter a lot more than the specialized tools that existed then. Spark was the vehicle for that thesis.

And I'll say, as an academic, it was also a bet on ourselves. Matei, Ali, Reynold, Patrick, Andy, Scott, all of us came out of the lab, and none of us had really run a company. There were plenty of people who told us we should license the technology to someone else. But we felt that if we didn't do it, the opportunity would get picked up by someone who cared less about the project. So in some ways the risk of not doing it felt bigger than the risk of doing it.

r001.rationale: The response calls Spark the engine that got Databricks started and a vehicle for its broader thesis, but does not say Spark’s success was the most likely route to the success of Databricks’ own product.

r002.rationale: It describes accepting business risks to keep Spark open, but does not prioritize a viable strategy over the easiest or shortest route to success.

r003.rationale: The response says Databricks did not want to be just a Spark company, describes a broader data-and-AI goal, and frames Spark as the starting engine for that ambition.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say we thought of it as betting the company on Spark alone. Spark was the starting point. The broader bet was that data was becoming central to every company, and that making it easier to process and analyze that data would be valuable.

Of course, an open-source project and a business are different things. People can be excited about the technology, but you still have to solve the operational problems: How do you make it reliable? How do you make it easy to use? How do you let a team get value from it without spending all its time managing infrastructure?

So the way we thought about it was: Spark gives us a foundation, but the company has to deliver something beyond that. You want to be committed to the problem customers have, while being willing to evolve the technology you use to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response calls Spark a starting point and foundation, but does not say Databricks viewed Spark’s success as the most likely route to its product’s success.

r002.rationale: It says to stay committed to customers’ problems and evolve the technology, but does not compare a viable strategy with the easiest or shortest route to success.

r003.rationale: It says Spark is a foundation and the company must deliver something beyond it, clearly indicating that major success would require expanding beyond Spark.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, at the time, it didn’t feel like we were making a bet on a technology that nobody wanted. We were already seeing people use Spark, and we believed there was a need for a better way to process data. The question was whether we could turn that interest into a business.

And that’s a different problem. An open-source project can be very successful, but companies need more than the software. They need something reliable, easy to use, something they don’t have to spend all their time operating. So our bet was that we could take Spark and make it accessible to a much broader set of users.

Of course, there was risk. But we had worked on the technology, we understood it, and we could see the problems people were trying to solve. That gave us the conviction to start.
